title: Numerical derivation 265: Laplace Transform & CT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 265)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. Derivations in this module therefore never quote X(s) alone: poles, zeros and ROC are derived together, partial fractions are inverted term by term with the ROC selecting right- or left-sided inverses, and stability is read from pole positions relative to the jw axis. The unilateral form additionally converts initial conditions into sources, which is what makes circuit problems mechanical.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Numerical derivation, parameter set 265)
Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: X(s) = integral x(t) e^{-st} dt ; H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) ; poles in LHP for causal stability. Every symbol is defined before use, units are carried, and no result is quoted without the relation that produces it.
Step 2 — Fix the parameter set. Parameter set 265 selects the numerical constants appearing in the evidence table below (derived deterministically from the set index, so this derivation can be regenerated and audited). Record the givens, the target quantity, and the model assumptions before any algebra.
Step 3 — Apply the definition literally. Substitute the entry's signal/system into the defining integral, sum, or transform — do not start from a memorised shortcut. Shortcuts are used only in Step 6 as an independent cross-check.
Step 4 — Evaluate in stages. Break the evaluation into the rows of the evidence table: each row is one abscissa (time, index, frequency, SNR, or bin), the quantity evaluated there, and a running or closed-form comparator evaluated in parallel.
Step 5 — Take the limit or closed form. Where the table accumulates (energy, partial sums, partial Fourier sums, convolution running sums), compare the accumulation against its closed form or limit and note the convergence behaviour explicitly.
Step 6 — Cross-check by an independent route. Re-derive the headline result through the module's property shortcut (symmetry, Parseval, convolution properties, pole location, Shannon-then-Nyquist ordering, or eigenvalue equivalence) and require agreement with Step 4.
Step 7 — Interrogate boundary cases. Ask what changes at the edges of validity: a pole crossing an axis or circle, fs falling below twice fm, mu exceeding 1, a non-rational Omega0 over 2 pi, or an ROC that excludes the stability contour. State the verdict change in one sentence.
Step 8 — Interpret physically. Translate the mathematics back into the system story: what decays, what rings, what folds, what saturates, and what a measurement would actually show.

title: Numerical derivation 265: z-Transform & DT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 265)

The z-transform is the discrete-time mirror of Laplace, with the unit circle playing the role of the jw axis. title: Numerical derivation 265: Fourier Series & Transform (CT) — worked from first principles (parameter set 265)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Fourier analysis re-expresses signals in the basis of eternal exponentials. For periodic signals the spectrum is a line spectrum whose coefficients come from one-period integrals and obey symmetry shortcuts and Parseval power bookkeeping; for aperiodic signals the transform is a density and convolution becomes multiplication, which is the entire basis of filtering. title: Numerical derivation 265: Waves, Channels & Data-Rate Limits — worked from first principles (parameter set 265)

Communication channels are governed by two complementary laws. Shannon's capacity, built from bandwidth and SNR, is an upper bound no coding can exceed in noise; Nyquist's formula turns a chosen rate into required signal levels on a noiseless channel. title: Numerical derivation 265: Modulation & Transmission — worked from first principles (parameter set 265)

title: Formal proof-style derivation 269: z-Transform & DT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 269)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The z-transform is the discrete-time mirror of Laplace, with the unit circle playing the role of the jw axis. These derivations emphasise the geometry: right-sided sequences converge outside their outermost pole, stability demands that the ROC include the unit circle, and causal stability collapses to the memorable picture of poles inside the circle. title: Numerical derivation 271: Signals & Classification — worked from first principles (parameter set 271)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A signal is information made measurable: a function of time whose shape can be classified before any system touches it. Fourier analysis re-expresses signals in the basis of eternal exponentials. For periodic signals the spectrum is a line spectrum whose coefficients come from one-period integrals and obey symmetry shortcuts and Parseval power bookkeeping; for aperiodic signals the transform is a density and convolution becomes multiplication, which is the entire basis of filtering. CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A system is a rule that maps inputs to outputs, and the five property tests (memory, causality, linearity, time-invariance, stability) are procedures, not adjectives. The formal pattern in this module is always the same: assume two arbitrary inputs and their outputs, form a combined or shifted input, push it through the rule, and compare against the required combination or shift of outputs. title: Numerical derivation 286: Laplace Transform & CT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 286)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. Derivations in this module therefore never quote X(s) alone: poles, zeros and ROC are derived together, partial fractions are inverted term by term with the ROC selecting right- or left-sided inverses, and stability is read from pole positions relative to the jw axis. The z-transform is the discrete-time mirror of Laplace, with the unit circle playing the role of the jw axis. CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A signal is information made measurable: a function of time whose shape can be classified before any system touches it. Classification is not taxonomy for its own sake; each class selects the correct mathematics. For periodic signals the spectrum is a line spectrum whose coefficients come from one-period integrals and obey symmetry shortcuts and Parseval power bookkeeping; for aperiodic signals the transform is a density and convolution becomes multiplication, which is the entire basis of filtering. CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Discrete-time spectra are periodic with period 2 pi, finite data produce the DFT's N bins, and sampling replicates spectra every fs so that overlap becomes aliasing. CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A system is a rule that maps inputs to outputs, and the five property tests (memory, causality, linearity, time-invariance, stability) are procedures, not adjectives. The formal pattern in this module is always the same: assume two arbitrary inputs and their outputs, form a combined or shifted input, push it through the rule, and compare against the required combination or shift of outputs. Equality for all inputs proves the property; a single counterexample disproves it, which is why each derivation ends with an explicit verdict and the boundary case that would change it.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Numerical derivation, parameter set 298)
Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: T{a x1 + b x2} = a T{x1} + b T{x2} ; delayed input must give delayed output. Every symbol is defined before use, units are carried, and no result is quoted without the relation that produces it.
Step 2 — Fix the parameter set. Parameter set 298 selects the numerical constants appearing in the evidence table below (derived deterministically from the set index, so this derivation can be regenerated and audited). Record the givens, the target quantity, and the model assumptions before any algebra.
Step 3 — Apply the definition literally. Substitute the entry's signal/system into the defining integral, sum, or transform — do not start from a memorised shortcut. Shortcuts are used only in Step 6 as an independent cross-check.
Step 4 — Evaluate in stages. Break the evaluation into the rows of the evidence table: each row is one abscissa (time, index, frequency, SNR, or bin), the quantity evaluated there, and a running or closed-form comparator evaluated in parallel.
Step 5 — Take the limit or closed form. Where the table accumulates (energy, partial sums, partial Fourier sums, convolution running sums), compare the accumulation against its closed form or limit and note the convergence behaviour explicitly.
Step 6 — Cross-check by an independent route. Re-derive the headline result through the module's property shortcut (symmetry, Parseval, convolution properties, pole location, Shannon-then-Nyquist ordering, or eigenvalue equivalence) and require agreement with Step 4.
Step 7 — Interrogate boundary cases. Ask what changes at the edges of validity: a pole crossing an axis or circle, fs falling below twice fm, mu exceeding 1, a non-rational Omega0 over 2 pi, or an ROC that excludes the stability contour. State the verdict change in one sentence.
Step 8 — Interpret physically. Translate the mathematics back into the system story: what decays, what rings, what folds, what saturates, and what a measurement would actually show.

title: Numerical derivation 298: Laplace Transform & CT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 298)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. Derivations in this module therefore never quote X(s) alone: poles, zeros and ROC are derived together, partial fractions are inverted term by term with the ROC selecting right- or left-sided inverses, and stability is read from pole positions relative to the jw axis. The unilateral form additionally converts initial conditions into sources, which is what makes circuit problems mechanical.

title: Numerical derivation 298: z-Transform & DT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 298)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The z-transform is the discrete-time mirror of Laplace, with the unit circle playing the role of the jw axis. These derivations emphasise the geometry: right-sided sequences converge outside their outermost pole, stability demands that the ROC include the unit circle, and causal stability collapses to the memorable picture of poles inside the circle. Difference equations become rational H(z) by term-by-term transformation, and inverse transforms are checked by power-series expansion so that algebra and sequence agree coefficient by coefficient.

title: Numerical derivation 298: Fourier Series & Transform (CT) — worked from first principles (parameter set 298)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Fourier analysis re-expresses signals in the basis of eternal exponentials. For periodic signals the spectrum is a line spectrum whose coefficients come from one-period integrals and obey symmetry shortcuts and Parseval power bookkeeping; for aperiodic signals the transform is a density and convolution becomes multiplication, which is the entire basis of filtering. title: Formal proof-style derivation 302: Convolution & LTI Response — worked from first principles (parameter set 302)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Convolution is the LTI engine: decompose the input into impulses, answer each impulse with a shifted impulse response, and sum. The derivations here move between the integral or sum definition, the graphical flip-shift-multiply-accumulate reading, and the algebraic properties (commutativity, distributivity, associativity) that let engineers reorder and merge systems. Modulation moves information onto a carrier by varying amplitude, frequency or phase, and digital keying quantises that variation into constellation points. These derivations expand AM products into carrier and sideband terms with power accounted watt by watt, apply bandwidth rules (double-sideband, Carson for FM) with their assumptions stated, and convert between baud and bit rate through bits per symbol, always returning to the constellation picture where distance between points explains noise immunity better than any slogan.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Theoretical derivation, parameter set 303)
Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: s_AM = Ac[1+mu m(t)] cos(wc t) ; BW_AM = 2 BWm ; BitRate = Baud x log2(L). Every symbol is defined before use, units are carried, and no result is quoted without the relation that produces it.
Step 2 — Fix the parameter set. Parameter set 303 selects the numerical constants appearing in the evidence table below (derived deterministically from the set index, so this derivation can be regenerated and audited). Record the givens, the target quantity, and the model assumptions before any algebra.
Step 3 — Apply the definition literally. Substitute the entry's signal/system into the defining integral, sum, or transform — do not start from a memorised shortcut. Shortcuts are used only in Step 6 as an independent cross-check.
Step 4 — Evaluate in stages. Break the evaluation into the rows of the evidence table: each row is one abscissa (time, index, frequency, SNR, or bin), the quantity evaluated there, and a running or closed-form comparator evaluated in parallel.
Step 5 — Take the limit or closed form. Where the table accumulates (energy, partial sums, partial Fourier sums, convolution running sums), compare the accumulation against its closed form or limit and note the convergence behaviour explicitly.
Step 6 — Cross-check by an independent route. Re-derive the headline result through the module's property shortcut (symmetry, Parseval, convolution properties, pole location, Shannon-then-Nyquist ordering, or eigenvalue equivalence) and require agreement with Step 4.
Step 7 — Interrogate boundary cases. Ask what changes at the edges of validity: a pole crossing an axis or circle, fs falling below twice fm, mu exceeding 1, a non-rational Omega0 over 2 pi, or an ROC that excludes the stability contour. State the verdict change in one sentence.
Step 8 — Interpret physically. Translate the mathematics back into the system story: what decays, what rings, what folds, what saturates, and what a measurement would actually show.

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A system is a rule that maps inputs to outputs, and the five property tests (memory, causality, linearity, time-invariance, stability) are procedures, not adjectives. The formal pattern in this module is always the same: assume two arbitrary inputs and their outputs, form a combined or shifted input, push it through the rule, and compare against the required combination or shift of outputs. title: Theoretical derivation 306: Laplace Transform & CT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 306)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. Derivations in this module therefore never quote X(s) alone: poles, zeros and ROC are derived together, partial fractions are inverted term by term with the ROC selecting right- or left-sided inverses, and stability is read from pole positions relative to the jw axis. The z-transform is the discrete-time mirror of Laplace, with the unit circle playing the role of the jw axis. title: Theoretical derivation 312: Signals & Classification — worked from first principles (parameter set 312)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A signal is information made measurable: a function of time whose shape can be classified before any system touches it. Classification is not taxonomy for its own sake; each class selects the correct mathematics. Periodic signals invite Fourier series, finite-energy signals invite the Fourier transform, and discrete-time signals force the periodicity question to pass through rationality of Omega0 over 2 pi. The derivations in this module therefore always begin by naming the class, then applying the class-specific integral or sum, then checking the result against the defining property.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Theoretical derivation, parameter set 312)

title: Numerical derivation 313: Fourier Series & Transform (CT) — worked from first principles (parameter set 313)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Fourier analysis re-expresses signals in the basis of eternal exponentials. For periodic signals the spectrum is a line spectrum whose coefficients come from one-period integrals and obey symmetry shortcuts and Parseval power bookkeeping; for aperiodic signals the transform is a density and convolution becomes multiplication, which is the entire basis of filtering. Derivations here compute coefficients from the integral definition, verify power in both domains, and interpret magnitude and phase spectra as instructions for what a filter will do.

title: Theoretical derivation 315: Elementary Signals & Operations — worked from first principles (parameter set 315)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Elementary signals are the atoms of the subject. The impulse extracts values through sifting, the step accumulates impulse area, the ramp accumulates the step, and exponentials rotate and scale through Euler's identity. Every complicated waveform in later modules is assembled from shifted, folded and scaled copies of these atoms, so each derivation here isolates one operation, performs it symbolically first, and only then substitutes numbers, keeping sign and shift errors visible rather than hiding them inside arithmetic.

title: Numerical derivation 319: Waves, Channels & Data-Rate Limits — worked from first principles (parameter set 319)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION

title: Numerical derivation 322: Convolution & LTI Response — worked from first principles (parameter set 322)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Convolution is the LTI engine: decompose the input into impulses, answer each impulse with a shifted impulse response, and sum. The derivations here move between the integral or sum definition, the graphical flip-shift-multiply-accumulate reading, and the algebraic properties (commutativity, distributivity, associativity) that let engineers reorder and merge systems. Each worked entry evaluates the defining sum directly, then re-derives the same answer through a property shortcut, because agreement between the two routes is the strongest available check.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Numerical derivation, parameter set 322)

title: Formal proof-style derivation 323: Modulation & Transmission — worked from first principles (parameter set 323)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Modulation moves information onto a carrier by varying amplitude, frequency or phase, and digital keying quantises that variation into constellation points. CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. Derivations in this module therefore never quote X(s) alone: poles, zeros and ROC are derived together, partial fractions are inverted term by term with the ROC selecting right- or left-sided inverses, and stability is read from pole positions relative to the jw axis. The unilateral form additionally converts initial conditions into sources, which is what makes circuit problems mechanical.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Numerical derivation, parameter set 325)
Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: X(s) = integral x(t) e^{-st} dt ; H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) ; poles in LHP for causal stability. Every symbol is defined before use, units are carried, and no result is quoted without the relation that produces it.
Step 2 — Fix the parameter set. Parameter set 325 selects the numerical constants appearing in the evidence table below (derived deterministically from the set index, so this derivation can be regenerated and audited). Record the givens, the target quantity, and the model assumptions before any algebra.
Step 3 — Apply the definition literally. Substitute the entry's signal/system into the defining integral, sum, or transform — do not start from a memorised shortcut. Shortcuts are used only in Step 6 as an independent cross-check.
Step 4 — Evaluate in stages. Break the evaluation into the rows of the evidence table: each row is one abscissa (time, index, frequency, SNR, or bin), the quantity evaluated there, and a running or closed-form comparator evaluated in parallel.
Step 5 — Take the limit or closed form. Where the table accumulates (energy, partial sums, partial Fourier sums, convolution running sums), compare the accumulation against its closed form or limit and note the convergence behaviour explicitly.
Step 6 — Cross-check by an independent route. Re-derive the headline result through the module's property shortcut (symmetry, Parseval, convolution properties, pole location, Shannon-then-Nyquist ordering, or eigenvalue equivalence) and require agreement with Step 4.
Step 7 — Interrogate boundary cases. Ask what changes at the edges of validity: a pole crossing an axis or circle, fs falling below twice fm, mu exceeding 1, a non-rational Omega0 over 2 pi, or an ROC that excludes the stability contour. State the verdict change in one sentence.
Step 8 — Interpret physically. Translate the mathematics back into the system story: what decays, what rings, what folds, what saturates, and what a measurement would actually show.

title: Numerical derivation 325: z-Transform & DT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 325)

The z-transform is the discrete-time mirror of Laplace, with the unit circle playing the role of the jw axis. title: Numerical derivation 325: Fourier Series & Transform (CT) — worked from first principles (parameter set 325)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Fourier analysis re-expresses signals in the basis of eternal exponentials. For periodic signals the spectrum is a line spectrum whose coefficients come from one-period integrals and obey symmetry shortcuts and Parseval power bookkeeping; for aperiodic signals the transform is a density and convolution becomes multiplication, which is the entire basis of filtering. title: Numerical derivation 325: Waves, Channels & Data-Rate Limits — worked from first principles (parameter set 325)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Communication channels are governed by two complementary laws. Shannon's capacity, built from bandwidth and SNR, is an upper bound no coding can exceed in noise; Nyquist's formula turns a chosen rate into required signal levels on a noiseless channel. title: Numerical derivation 325: Modulation & Transmission — worked from first principles (parameter set 325)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. title: Theoretical derivation 327: State-Space Analysis — worked from first principles (parameter set 327)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
State-space models package a system's memory into a state vector so that dynamics become matrix algebra: x-dot equals A x plus B u, y equals C x plus D u. A system is a rule that maps inputs to outputs, and the five property tests (memory, causality, linearity, time-invariance, stability) are procedures, not adjectives. The formal pattern in this module is always the same: assume two arbitrary inputs and their outputs, form a combined or shifted input, push it through the rule, and compare against the required combination or shift of outputs. Equality for all inputs proves the property; a single counterexample disproves it, which is why each derivation ends with an explicit verdict and the boundary case that would change it.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Formal proof-style derivation, parameter set 338)
Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: T{a x1 + b x2} = a T{x1} + b T{x2} ; delayed input must give delayed output. Every symbol is defined before use, units are carried, and no result is quoted without the relation that produces it.
Step 2 — Fix the parameter set. Parameter set 338 selects the numerical constants appearing in the evidence table below (derived deterministically from the set index, so this derivation can be regenerated and audited). Record the givens, the target quantity, and the model assumptions before any algebra.

Step 4 — Evaluate in stages. Break the evaluation into the rows of the evidence table: each row is one abscissa (time, index, frequency, SNR, or bin), the quantity evaluated there, and a running or closed-form comparator evaluated in parallel.
Step 5 — Take the limit or closed form. Where the table accumulates (energy, partial sums, partial Fourier sums, convolution running sums), compare the accumulation against its closed form or limit and note the convergence behaviour explicitly.
Step 6 — Cross-check by an independent route. Re-derive the headline result through the module's property shortcut (symmetry, Parseval, convolution properties, pole location, Shannon-then-Nyquist ordering, or eigenvalue equivalence) and require agreement with Step 4.
Step 7 — Interrogate boundary cases. Ask what changes at the edges of validity: a pole crossing an axis or circle, fs falling below twice fm, mu exceeding 1, a non-rational Omega0 over 2 pi, or an ROC that excludes the stability contour. State the verdict change in one sentence.

title: Formal proof-style derivation 338: Laplace Transform & CT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 338)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. Derivations in this module therefore never quote X(s) alone: poles, zeros and ROC are derived together, partial fractions are inverted term by term with the ROC selecting right- or left-sided inverses, and stability is read from pole positions relative to the jw axis. title: Formal proof-style derivation 338: z-Transform & DT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 338)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The z-transform is the discrete-time mirror of Laplace, with the unit circle playing the role of the jw axis. These derivations emphasise the geometry: right-sided sequences converge outside their outermost pole, stability demands that the ROC include the unit circle, and causal stability collapses to the memorable picture of poles inside the circle. CONCEPT AND INTUITION

For periodic signals the spectrum is a line spectrum whose coefficients come from one-period integrals and obey symmetry shortcuts and Parseval power bookkeeping; for aperiodic signals the transform is a density and convolution becomes multiplication, which is the entire basis of filtering. title: Theoretical derivation 339: Waves, Channels & Data-Rate Limits — worked from first principles (parameter set 339)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Communication channels are governed by two complementary laws. Shannon's capacity, built from bandwidth and SNR, is an upper bound no coding can exceed in noise; Nyquist's formula turns a chosen rate into required signal levels on a noiseless channel.
